items.body: Shell and Core takes its title from the unfinished concrete structures that have become fixtures of the Syrian landscape, and Tasgeelat Al-Husni تسجيلات الحُسني uses that image of arrested construction as a way of looking at lives left incomplete. Much of the record is assembled from things heard or observed in everyday life: bureaucratic rituals, checkpoints, cars, street conversations, scrap collectors and an uncle’s absurd political opinions. On “Spacetune” these details accumulate into a comic story that deliberately goes nowhere; “Existing” turns repetition and waiting into its subject, while the heavier “Grinder” pushes familiar material towards something more grotesque. The humour is important. Rather than presenting Syria exclusively through catastrophe, Tasgeelat Al-Husni draws on a local tradition of satire and everyday mockery in which absurdity is one means of living with circumstances that have themselves become absurd. The music operates in much the same way, refusing a clean division between local tradition and experimental electronics. The oud can introduce the relatively spacious “Existing”, sit behind electronic and guitar noise on “Spacetune”, or grind against doom-laden riffs on “Grinder”. Al-Husni explicitly rejects using the instrument as a nostalgic signifier of a disappearing culture; here it belongs to the present as naturally as synthesis, distortion or field recording. Progressive and heavy rock are equally embedded in the record’s vocabulary, particularly in its abrupt shifts between calm and physical weight. Lazar Mečanin’s production makes those contrasts unusually pronounced: passages of relative openness can suddenly thicken into distortion, low-frequency pressure and noise, giving the album the unstable logic of the environment it describes. One of the album’s most striking changes of register comes on “Perspective”, where the voice of Ukrainian opera singer Oksana Vakula introduces a radiant tone, briefly opening up the record’s otherwise rough and unstable sonic terrain. That makes the unfinished Massar Discovery Center on the cover more than an illustration. Along with Syria’s other abandoned concrete shells, it becomes an architectural counterpart to a record about interrupted trajectories. Yet Shell and Core avoids turning incompletion into a grand metaphor. What matters most is the peripheral and the discarded: things overheard, jokes, irritating routines, incongruous sounds and surreal encounters. The picture of Syria that emerges is at the same time damaged and precarious, but also mundane and funny, a place whose exposed structural bones are filled with everyday life. To help us better understand the production process for Shell and Core we reached out directly to Tasgeelat Al-Husni. Throughout عَ العَضم (Shell and Core), everyday Syrian life is depicted in a way that often feels almost surreal, allowing the ordinary and the mythical to coexist. The repeated “unknown” in “Spacetune”, the taxi driver nicknamed Azrael—the Angel of Death—blasting heavy dabke, the endless bureaucracy of “Existing”, the Ladas, and finally the litany of scrap collectors all feel like fragments of the same social landscape. There is also a distinctly sardonic humour running through the writing. Do you think of your lyrics as poetry, documentary montage, social commentary or simply another way of composing with sound? Most of the lyrics are rephrasing of something I have heard in Syria either in a conversation with friends or randomly on the street. I wrote down some of what I had heard and then integrated them with how I thought of each song. I am new to writing words, so I don’t know much, but I have tried writing a comical story with mild suspense that leads nowhere on “Spacetune,” describing recurrent scenes from daily life on “Existing,” and creating some surreal visual scenes on “Grinder.” The sardonic humor is essential to the environment where the album came from. It’s in the music we hear (such as the music of the Rahbani family), the TV we watch (such as Spotlight – بقعة ضوء), the books we read (such as Muhammad al-Maghut’s), so you would also hear it in your day-to-day life from your relatives, your college friends, the bus driver or even from a soldier on a checkpoint. Add to that the absurdity of people’s takes on the conflict, like that uncle on Spacetune, which naturally calls for mockery. Peugeot 504 – photo by Hussain Hussain The second track, “Existing”, opens with an oud before gradually expanding into a much broader electronic landscape. The instrument never feels nostalgic or symbolic of tradition; instead, it becomes another texture within the composition. Was it important for you to avoid treating the oud as a marker of cultural identity, allowing it instead to coexist naturally with electronics and noise? It was! I think such instruments are not supposed to sound like a distant cry from the past echoing in an empty space, or “a ghostly remnant from a lost culture”, like David Byrne once wrote. The oud, like any instrument, should be used to serve the song the way the song is meant to be. It definitely could be used in its classical character with takasim and as accompaniment for singing like on “Existing,” but it can also accompany heavy doom metal riffs to add a bloody drilling texture on “Grinder,” or do some finger picking behind synth and guitar noises like on Spacetune. If you listen to a based folk performance from the past, you hear the oud vital and integrated with the rest of the instruments, not sounding like an anomaly, and I think this is how it should be treated in any other (modern) context. Window – photo by Hussain Hussain Although the album is rooted in electroacoustic composition and experimental electronics, there are moments—particularly in the treatment of distortion, low-frequency weight and rhythmic pressure—that recall progressive rock, heavy rock and noise. Are those traditions part of your musical vocabulary, and how do they intersect with the experimental and electronic music you make today? These traditions strongly influence how we have approached this record and music making in general. The treatment of sound at this level was more Lazar’s part, so I have forwarded the question to him, and this is his response: “Those traditions have to be a part of our vocabulary given the fact it’s the music we grew up on – Floyd, Crimson, etc. These bands influenced us as players but they also influenced how we think about music. A song can exhibit cinematic properties and sometimes be even more immersive than a movie if done right. The record is really a landscape representing every-day life in Syria (if I understood it correctly myself hah), moments of beauty and calmness intertwined with unpredictable chaos mostly right next to each other, so in a way the music is interpreting life, and by using these acoustic and production techniques we are attempting to recreate the feelings one might have simply living there.” Random Structure – photo by Hussain Hussain How do you see your work in relation to other Syrian experimental musicians? Is there a shared aesthetic or set of concerns emerging from the scene, or do you feel that each artist is responding to the experiences of recent years in fundamentally different ways? I have learned a lot from contemporary Syrian and Arab artists — Tootard, Shabjdeed, Khaled Allaf, Lynn Adib, Al-Rahel Al-Kabir, Kulna Sawa, and many more — and that has encouraged me to work on my own stuff, sing about what I have heard or seen, and eventually release that. It is true that everyone is responding to their experiences in their own way; some express that in a desperate way, some in a cynical way, some tackle social issues, and some speak about personal experiences. Maybe what we have in common is our frustration and disgust with our situation now and in recent years, but who knows? What’s important to me is that many of our artists sound so fresh, so unique and so relevant, and I always look forward to hearing their new approaches and what they are talking about. The cover features the unfinished Massar Discovery Center (“Massar Rose”) in Damascus—a project that was meant to embody education, innovation and the future before construction stopped in 2014. Throughout the album, there is a recurring sense of lives shaped by interruption: bureaucratic waiting, checkpoints, abandoned trajectories and systems that never quite reach completion. Did you see the building as encapsulating that condition, or were you drawn to it for different reasons? Gardenia Towers – photo by Hussain Hussain Exactly, hence the name, ع العضم Shell and Core! The rest of the album art (partly prepared for a CD release) features some well-known incomplete buildings, such as the infamous 50-year-old Yalbugha Tower in the middle of the capital and the Gardenia Towers in Homs that became known among the public as the “Death Towers”, used by snipers during the war. Such giant incomplete, mostly ugly, structures are so common to see in Syria. They are ironically reflective of the life of Syrian individual that has become so crippled, it might never reach a sense of completion. Everyone who lost their home forever and had to live in a tent, everyone that lost their beloved ones, got detained for the stupidest reason, or had to serve in the army for 8 years or so, and also everyone who just had to live or grow up there during these awful times. To me, this building not only encapsulates these incomplete trajectories, but also resembles, with its bare bones (عضم) sticking out, how naked, exposed and fragile we are. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Achachay is what highland Ecuadorians say when the cold catches them, arraray when the heat does. Both words came into Andean Spanish from Quichua, and BRITTA builds “Achachay” on the pair: a love song about wanting someone enough to feel both. A requinto line, the small high-tuned guitar of Ecuadorian string music, runs over percussion drawn from the country’s Pacific coast and a trap low end. The alt-pop production leaves the guitar exposed and the beat holds a steady pressure under a vocal that stays at the point of anticipation. Born in Ambato in the central Ecuadorian Andes and based in Los Angeles in the US, Britta has been feeding Ecuadorian traditional forms into dance production for a while: on her single “NON3 (no te dejes avecilla)” she sampled her own voice singing an albazo, the fast triple-time song form of the Ecuadorian highlands, and built a house track around it. “Achachay” points that same working method at Latin alternative, with the Andean Spanish idioms running through the lyric carrying as much of the song’s identity as the requinto and the percussion do. Listen to “Achachay” HERE The post Daily Discovery: BRITTA – Achachay appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — A south Korean group that took 18 years to release their first album and the least one can say isthat Superstring didn't take the easy road. Yes their main influence is classical music, but theywouldn't name have named their kids Ludwig, Johan Sebastian or Wolfgang Amadeus. They might havethought of Edgar, Karlheinz or Gabriel, though. BTW, it's not just about modern classical , as thereare hints of jazz dispersed throughout the duration of their first works. Noteworthy, TGD was firstreleased as vinyl-only, waiting some three years to finally release it in the user-friendly formatcalled CD.Indeed, while relatively dissonant, SS is not extreme Avant Prog like Guapo would be, but they'renot very careful about your sanity beyond your eardrums. Their Grand Design is still relativelyaccessible, if you like atmospheric improvisation, almost cinematic, gloomy ambiances with also PostRock moments. This instrumental quintet will be remarkably stable throughout their career, focusingon the violin and piano as lead instruments, but backed up by a guitar. There are some lovelymoments, but also plenty of tense passages, not necessarily providing a release outlet for thenervous accumulation.TBH, not my cup or tea, but it's definitely worth their Bandcamp detour at least once, even if itwill never be an essential piece of work. Add another half-star, though !!!

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — There is so much talent involved in making this record that though it escapes the normal blues/psychedelia forms of that era and becomes proggy and avant, it is so easy and fun to listen too. It takes you through so many emotions, it can make you angry, it's bluesy, it's funny at parts (has a track on dedicated to a candy bar).But man, although the musicianship is of course fantastic, Captain's vocal performance makes the real difference here. Just listen to songs like "Where there's woman" , "Grown so ugly", "Autumn's child", or "Electricity" (where he literally broke a microphone while recording it.)Although Zappa was a good friend and inspiration to Captain Beefheart, Captain's music is far more accessible and this album is a good starting point for a listener who wants to discover their music.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The use of synthesizers and the Mellotron, combined with an abrasive, dense hard rock sound, defined Black Bonzo's debut as progressive hard rock; vocalist Magnus Lindgren, with his very clean voice, and keyboardist Nicklas Ahlund, capable of playing everything from rock 'n' roll to classical organ passages, evoke the more daring side of Deep Purple, while on the title track, "Lady of the Light," they also create an almost cinematic, eerie atmosphere."Brave Young Soldier" also features psychedelia, rhythmic shifts, and dissonances that greatly enrich the track; once again, Magnus Lindgren demonstrates his own distinct personality and style, avoiding the path of other singers in the genre. Guitar and organ combine for a brilliant riff at the end, blending a medieval past with rock music evocative of spells and stone forests."Fantasy World" evoked a different atmosphere, reminiscent of Wishbone Ash; "Freedom," on the other hand, could easily have appeared on Queen's debut album. The melody ultimately took center stage, a gothic, operatic tune that kept evolving. While this didn't necessarily contribute to the album's cohesion, the diversity added emotional depth, featuring the Mellotron from "Sirens" and, above all, the drumming, which, combined with the acoustic guitar, recalled King Crimson's debut.On one hand, there is the clenched-teeth rock and tight sound of "Jailbait," and the dark, ominous lyricism of "Leave Your Burdens", complete with Black Sabbath-style riffs reminiscent of their bluesier moments, while the hypnotic conclusion of "Where the River Meets the Sea" serves as the perfect finale. It clearly defines an artistic vision that was at once velvet and steel, possessing scales and gills to dive through the ocean, yet also lungs to scream and fill with air in order to fly.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — *Limite Acque Sicure* by *Limite Acque Sicure*?a surprising title and surname, a sort of metaphor with multiple possible levels of meaning: the cartographic contours of the Mediterranean Sea in the Middle Ages? A body of water of a certain depth, not to be exceeded? The knowledge of our inner selves (or that of others), beyond which it may be dangerous to venture? The need to push past our own limits in order to grow? Or simply the name of a red wine from Abruzzo? Please refer to the very interesting lyrics on this album for a hint of an answer (be sure to have an Italian translation tool on hand if you don't speak the language). Musically speaking, you don't need to be an expert on Banco's music to understand that *Limite Acque Sicure*, hailing from Ferrara and formed in 2005 by singer Andrea Chendi and keyboardist Antonello Giovannelli as just one of many tribute bands, is a true devotee of the golden age of the Nocenzi brothers' band?a fact confirmed by the inclusion on this self-titled album of the iconic "Il Giardino Del Mago" (Banco 1972), in a dazzling live version.Between the introductory "Sogno D'Oriente" (12:48)?with its oriental sounds, as its name suggests, reminiscent of the famous "Kashmir"?and the short "Ti Salver� " (2:11)?placed at the other end, in the style and spirit of Banco's "Traccia II" (that album again) Certain tracks on *Limite Acque Sicure* stand out more. These are the ones where the band most clearly demonstrates that it has something personal to convey to us. "Terra Straniera" (7:53), with its majestic, enthusiastic, and determined finale, is closer in style to *Prowlers* than to *Banco*; "Il Respiro Dell'Anima" (8:25), with its more lively rhythm, ambitious structure, and shimmering arrangements that leave plenty of room for highly effective guitar and Moog solos. And above all, the epic "Fiamme Intorno " (10:48), with a darker main theme (though carried by a deceptively light rhythm), as if weighed down by a relentless exploration of humanity's spiritual wanderings, then giving way to a second, more open and luminous section, full of hope, whose coda?and this is quite unexpected?features a few drum beats dedicated to? Neil Peart. On a more contemporary note, the music of Limite Acque Sicure evokes memories of Museo Rosenbach, Campo Di Marte, Il Rovescio Della Medaglia, Alphataurus, and Apoteosi, all those meteor-like bands that shone for the duration of a single album (often released in 1973) before disappearing for a long time?or forever. "Limite Acque Sicure" seems to be a tribute to the RPI of the past, yet one that looks toward the future. In other words, it is less a relic of a glorious past than a promise of what the RPI may have in store.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Reale Accademia Di Musica is a italien band from Rome, best known among us for its self-titled debut album released in 1972, an Italian progressive rock sound similar to that of PFM from the same era, though lacking the Milanese band's charisma. The rest of their discography, led by composer Adriano Monteduro under the acronym RAM, is of much less interest to us? until their 2018 revival spearheaded by Pericle Sponzilli, the band's original guitarist, who enlisted the talents of virtuoso keyboardist Fabio Liberatori (a prolific composer of Italian film scores) and Erika Savastani, a young singer with a powerful voice, to release *Angeli Mutanti* that year?an interesting, if not essential, fusion of modern Italian pop and flamboyant, timeless Italian progressive rock.*Lame Di Luce* is in the same vein, while at times drawing closer to the Italian neo-prog of the '90s (Leviathan, Mad Crayon?) as on the magnificent "Ascesa al Fuji," one of those gems that seems to smile at us and make life so sweet as it comes alive with vibrant colors. Fifty years later, the pastoral feel of the debut album is very much present on "Onde di Sabbia," and a few other echoes of the RPI masters charm us effortlessly (Le Orme on "Due Pietre Preziose Birmane" or Banco on the jazzy "Si Parler�"). This band excels at writing melodies that are out of the ordinary while remaining accessible to a wide audience, as heard on the irresistible "Lame di Luce," which seems to be to Italian song what the Moody Blues' music was to English prog: sophisticated pop without being ostentatious, capable of sounding harmonious even to the most delicate angels in heaven. The final quarter-hour of *Lame di Luce* may seem a bit weaker. "Una Ferita da Disinfettare" is a well-crafted symphonic prog track, but it will primarily catch our attention for a brief, unexpected quote from the famous guitar solo in "Firth of Fifth." "Ore Lente" could pass for a simple, dynamic song with a catchy chorus, and "Incontri" for a nostalgic Pink Floyd-style ballad that's a bit too slow?were it not for the cinematic influence of Fabio Liberatori, which enriches the mood and atmosphere of both tracks.Ultimately, the best moments carry the album and overshadow the few, quite excusable weaknesses, ensuring that our favorable opinion remains. *Lame di Luce* is a pleasant surprise and deserves our full attention. All it needs are a few more instrumental developments to make it an excellent modern RPI album worthy of its illustrious predecessors, among whom *Reale Accademia Di Musica* was counted in the early '70s.

Is it the lyrics? Is it the keys? Is it something else? Maybe it is all these things combined. Now this record, has all that trademark elements of that era, it's bluesy, it's heavy, it's dark in some moments and happy on other moments, it's progy. "Repent Walpurgis" is an amazing instrumental and one of my favorites from that era. Matthew Fisher on the hammond, give me that same feeling, Jon Lord (Deep Purple) or Ken Hensley (Uriah Heep) give me when I'm listening to their records. Yes lads, it is that good.Procol Harum, as a typical British band, decided to leave "A whiter shade of pale" off of the UK vinyl release and put it just on the North America release, plus they left some amazing songs as bonus tracks. (Just listen "Homburg"!!!)A must listen for the fans of that era.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — SS's second album certainly starts in a WTF, but if Elements of Architecture stretches their TGD debut by a mile, and go the extra-distance to play on the dissonance frontier, but never crossing it. BTW, they must have a fascination about construction design, since their next three releases will mention it on the record sleeves. On the sonic front, it seems that Kim's bass guitar is playing a more prominent role than previously - especially on the title track. In a general way, Kim seems to be the head honcho, handling design & mixing/production, even, if the album is released again on the violinist Dancing Butterfly label. In some moments, via the guitarist, King Crimson is not far away.Definitely a harder grasp on what SS tried to do in this Avant-Post-Prog creation, but if all tracks were more in the mould of Floating Debris, then then they might've gotten that fourth star. .

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Third album in three years after taking 18 years to create their first one, Architecture might sound/read like a logical successor to their previous one, but there is quite a sonic progression here;eve,n if SS' collective paws are plainly recognizable. Indeed, we've taken a steep turn away from Avant-Prog, but I"m not sure this is due to the new arrival Katie's saxophone on three tracks, because it doesn't really change the overall soundscapes, even if the energy reach a different level and intensity - for the better, I might add. But indeed, the general sonic direction of this album tells us that we are at a corner of the band's career.The dissonance element present in their first two albums has almost disappeared, and this helps the accessibility o�f their music. Relatively absent from their first two album, there is a sense of drama permeating most of the tracks, endearing us to their musical escapes and extravaganzas. Emotional melodies over tight rhythms. BTW, it was their first album directly sold in CD, and for both formats, SS took the carte to make an attractive sleeve with a transparent protecting plastic sleeve. TBH, I really don't know why the band will change its name and record label (I guess the departure of their violinist played a big role), after the release of their best-yet album . But there will be two undeniable links: the Architecture link (purposely misspelled) and the same type of line-up (new violinist) and a now-permanent sax player replacing the too-discreet guitarist. but that's for their next album. In the meantime, their third is definitely the one I preferred at the time.

items.body: Review by Warthur — Bakerloo's sole album reveals them as a truly diverse progressive group of the early prog era. They've clearly emerged from the same blues rock primordial soup formented by the Yardbirds and Bluesbreakers and Cream and which saw peers like Jetbro Tull and Black Sabbath emerge. Bakerloo actually shared a manager with Sabbath, but it's Tull who you'll be reminded of most - in particular, the sound of their earliest days, before Mick Abrahams left. There's no flute, but plenty of harmonica - and the power trip work in enough influences from jazz and classical music to suggest a group just as broad in influences as Tull, though perhaps with more influence from the calmer, more meditative side of psychedelia creeping in at points.It's no surprise that they fell by the wayside at the end - this was a crowded scene, after all, and it was all too easy for groups to get lost in the shuffle, and with Tull already evolving away from their early blues influences and Black Sabbath turning the blues into doom metal their peers were moving to distinguish themselves, so you can see why Bakerloo were in danger of being eclipsed. In retrospect, it's a gem of its particular scene - it's just that the scene in question was on the cusp of being overtaken by other strands of prog and blues-derived rock.

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Recorded simultaneously with its hostile and murky counterpart, "Deliverance", during the summer of 2002, the gentler and more melancholic "Damnation" - Opeth's seventh album - didn't see the light of day until April 2003, due to their record label's decision to separate the two releases for commercial reasons. An album unexpectedly devoid of Mikael �kerfeldt's guttural vocals, the brutal riffs and abrasive textures that had defined the Swedish band, and their usual monolithic instrumental displays, the result of �kerfeldt's deliberate intention to immerse himself in the smoother, more experimental side of 1970s progressive rock, accompanied for this purpose by the fantastic Steven Wilson, whose decisive work as co-producer and musician brings a sensibility and sonic aesthetic that resonate with those of his band, Porcupine Tree.While it's true that in their earlier work Opeth included acoustic and refreshing sections amid their stormy arrangements, on "Damnation" they take it a step further by devoting its just over forty-three minutes to dreamy melodies set in an introspective and tense atmosphere that flows unhurriedly over the misty, ethereal soundscapes woven by Wilson's Mellotrons and Peter Lindgren's clean, serene guitars. Tracks like the hypnotic "Windowpane," with its magnificent jazz-inspired solo, or the psychedelic "In My Time of Need," "Death Whispered a Lullaby," and "Closure" evoke the most dreamlike and hazy side of genre icons such as King Crimson, the pre-"The Dark Side of the Moon" Pink Floyd, and the Gabriel-era Genesis.And staying true to that evocative, immersive vibe, the instrumental "Ending Credits," with its long guitar bends reminiscent of Camel's Andy Latimer, and the impeccable backing -as throughout the album- from the standout Mart�n M�ndez on bass and Martin Lopez on percussion, along with the trance-like and unchanging "Weakness," featuring a whispering, spectral �kerfeldt, ultimately round out "Damnation": the beginning of Opeth's stylistic transition and one of the most controversial phases of their career.3.5/4 stars

items.body: Review by alainPP — An evolving, melodic, synth-driven sound; the track evokes human degradation in the face of AI."Tears Of The Muse" kicks off as a dark, mid-tempo rock track featuring 80s-style keyboards?somewhere between rock, prog, and dark wave. A thunderous beat reminiscent of Genesis and Gabriel gives way to a sharp riff and vocals that trade lines with a vocoder. "EKO" features a hook redolent of Saga?think sugary new-millennium prog-metal with Martin stepping in for Damian. A dash of Arena, a touch of Lalu?it works perfectly for this groovy track with its driving bassline. "I Am The One" features piano accompanying Simon's metronomic drumming. It has a rich, proggy sound?like Toto?complemented by a heavy riff and a solo from Joop. There's a groovy, jazzy, Yes-style break leading into a warm choral finale. "Mayacama" is an instrumental that channels Toto and Saga?I can't help but hear the resemblance. A guitar groove underpins the melody, building into a progressive crescendo with the keyboards following suit. A piano break and a synth-led ballad section precede Joop showing off his dexterity. "Prince With The Swift Warning" features rolling pads and vocal harmonies that add complexity, navigating between rock, pop, and ballad styles. It includes a tense break with a sharp guitar solo, an infectious rhythm, and a second solo that is delicate, bluesy, and proggy."Learning To Fly" features airy vocals and echoes of Saga?or even Marillion. It's an accessible track that surprises with its evolution, while a dark organ keeps the listener on edge. The guitar solo is pure prog, leading into a riff where Martin shows off his impressive vocal range, backed by Simon. The finale soars as Joop and then Vivien drive the track to a spine-tingling climax. "A Drop Of Water" is an acoustic guitar interlude featuring a brilliant, ear-piercing arpeggio?a nod to Steve Howe of Yes. "Fhloston Paradise"?named after the station in *The Fifth Element*?blends hard-hitting rock and vocoder with the energetic, percussive groove characteristic of Joop, reminiscent of Iron Maiden. It features a Yes-style coda, confirming Vivien's admiration for the band. "Cordal Weaves" is a unique track with ethereal, searching notes and a stereo soundscape that creates a distinctly progressive atmosphere. It offers a funky, simmering moment: Martin rallies the energy, Joop lays into the rhythm, and Simon unleashes a barrage of drums. The finale features soaring vocals and a guitar full of melancholic longing. "Midnight Ink" serves as a piano-bar-style closer, driven by a poignant, whispered croon. Melancholic strings lend the track a solemn tone?the perfect way to wrap up the album.A melting pot of mainstream rock in the vein of Saga, Yes, and Toto, created above all for the sheer joy of it. It offers a softer take on prog metal and an intense jazz-prog vibe that feels like a journey in a time capsule.

items.body: Review by sgtpepper — After a long-term hiatus (last good album released in 1981), Collegium Musicum returned at least to the stage in 1997 with the original members of which Freso remained in a particular good shape. The choice of tracks performed was good as it didn't only feature the first two albums but reached later into their career. I am personally a bigger fan of their 1971-1975 period rather than their first eponymous album.The guest Andrej Seban provides elastic guitar while Hajek hasn't lost his edge on the drums.I'm not very content with Varga though because I find his playing somehow sloppy - as if he couldn't hit all the right keys, or not always on time. This suspicion raised with me in the beginning of the first track but hasn't evaporated later. Or is it just the not keyboard sound which does not allow for careful key distinction?In any case, this was the first official live album with their classic songs, however the double live album from 2010 could be more appealing.

items.body: BY GLOWBALL Since launching in 2024, GLOWBALL FESTIVAL has placed electronic music at its core, combining music, visual art, performance, subculture, and international exchange. Over the past three years, GLOWBALL has evolved from a festival rooted in global dance music culture and interdisciplinary creation into a longer-term practice encompassing international curation, artist collaboration, and exchange between cultural scenes. By 2026, GLOWBALL’s activities had expanded beyond the annual festival itself. In May, the team and participating artists travelled to Lyon, France, to collaborate with and perform at Nuits sonores. In June, GLOWBALL returned to Taipei for its third edition, followed in August by participation in talks, exhibitions, and international industry exchange at TMEX. From Taiwan to Lyon and back to Taipei, this journey across several months gradually outlined GLOWBALL’s evolving role as a platform for electronic music culture. Rather than repeating the same festival format from year to year, GLOWBALL continuously reconsiders the relationships between electronic music and other creative disciplines, cultural communities, and international networks. Music remains both the central artistic medium and a means through which these connections can be formed. 2024: Building a Foundation for Cross-Disciplinary Encounters through Global Dance Music Culture The name GLOWBALL began as a play on the word “global,” combining the luminous imagery of “glow” with the multiple associations of “ball”—a dance, a sphere, and a gathering. From the outset, GLOWBALL was never confined to a particular genre of electronic music. Instead, it explored how artists and practices from different regions, cultural backgrounds, and creative disciplines could coexist within a shared festival environment. International and Taiwanese musicians, DJs, new media artists, dancers, and performers were brought together under the same event, allowing the festival to become a site where different cultural practices could intersect. From its first edition, Ballroom culture, Indigenous culture, new media art, A/V live performance, contemporary dance, and electronic music all formed part of GLOWBALL’s landscape. Rather than defining itself through a single musical genre, the festival developed a framework centered on electronic music while allowing different cultures and creative methodologies to exist side by side. 2025: From Coexistence to Collaboration—Developing Cross-Disciplinary Production Methods The second edition, based on the theme of “Ping Pong”, placed greater emphasis on collaboration and interaction. Rather than simply bringing diverse acts together under one lineup, GLOWBALL paired them up to create shared performances. Electronic music was combined with traditional instrumentation, dance, artificial intelligence, motion capture, A/V live performance, and other disciplines. Through the joint production of different sounds, cultures, and artistic practices, interdisciplinary collaboration became an important part of GLOWBALL’s approach. That year, the festival worked with collectives and communities representing different cities and subcultural scenes, including HE.SHE.THEY., Over My Body, TYO GQOM, and Formosa Sound System. This broadened GLOWBALL’s focus beyond individual performers to include their cultural scenes as part of the programme too. International electronic music and party communities met local Taiwanese networks around sound system culture, Ballroom, drag, and queer culture, creating opportunities for both coexistence and exchange within the festival. GLOWBALL thus began moving beyond conventional festival programming centered on booking individual artists, developing instead into a platform connecting different cultural scenes. 2026: Building Two-Way International Exchange and Long-Term Networks The third edition built upon the previous year’s collaborations with different scenes and collectives, while expanding these relationships into longer-term exchanges across cities and national borders. The collaboration with Lyon-based Nuits sonores began in May, when GLOWBALL travelled to Lyon to curate performances and exchange programmes. It continued in June, when Nuits sonores Artistic Director Pierre Zeimet travelled to Taiwan to participate in the festival and a public conversation, creating a genuinely two-way curatorial relationship. At the same time, GLOWBALL continued to develop programmes in collaboration with different cultural scenes. Formosa Sound System once again created an independent sonic environment rooted in sound system culture. Taiwanese-Japanese art collective TOTEI brought together party culture and new media art through exhibitions, VJ performances, and late-night programming. Communities including isaNight, Ballroom, and drag performers also continued to take part, bringing local and international artists and audiences together on the same platform. Compared with the stage-based and scene-based collaborations of the previous year, partnerships in 2026 began to expand into co-curation, artist exchange, exhibition production, and knowledge sharing. Internationalization, in this sense, is no longer simply about increasing the number of overseas artists on the line-up. It is a process of gradually building sustained working relationships between different cities, cultural organizations, and creative communities. From Lyon in May and Taipei in June to continued industry and curatorial exchanges at TMEX in August, GLOWBALL has gradually evolved from an annual music festival into a platform connecting Taiwanese creators, Asian cultural scenes, and international cultural networks. Electronic Music as a Meeting Point for Different Cultural Scenes Global club, bass music, gqom, house, techno, experimental electronics, live music, traditional instrumentation, and various forms of cross-genre creation have all appeared throughout different editions of GLOWBALL. Rather than using genre as the festival’s primary organizing principle, GLOWBALL approaches electronic music as a cultural interface — a space through which different creative communities can encounter one another and form new relationships. DJs and dancers, musicians and new media artists, Ballroom and drag communities, Taiwanese creators and international curators each operate within their own professional networks and cultural contexts. A festival can create a shared time and space in which these otherwise separate networks begin to overlap. From Producing Programs to Building Cultural Networks Taiwan has active communities across independent music, new media art, DJ and VJ culture, dance, performance, and a wide range of subcultures. New creators and cultural practices continue to emerge. Yet different disciplines often have their own languages, audiences, and professional networks. Cross-disciplinary collaboration—as well as longer-term exchange with other Asian cities and European cultural scenes—requires time and sustained commitment. Over the past three years, GLOWBALL has therefore gradually placed greater emphasis not only on programming, but also on building relationships: connecting different music and art scenes, maintaining exchanges with international festivals and curatorial organizations, facilitating interdisciplinary co-production, and creating opportunities for creators from different cultural networks to meet and collaborate. These efforts are not intended to represent Taiwan’s electronic music culture as a whole, and GLOWBALL itself remains in an ongoing process of exploration and learning. Rather, the festival hopes to serve as one small but sustainable node within a much larger cultural network — continuously creating possibilities for exchange between artists, communities, and international networks within the scope of what it can realistically contribute. Looking Ahead GLOWBALL is currently preparing and exploring the next stage of its development. Moving forward, it will continue to take electronic music as a point of departure while expanding collaborations with different artistic disciplines, cultural communities, and international partners. These directions are still taking shape, and GLOWBALL looks forward to continuing to develop new possibilities for exchange and collaboration with like-minded artists, curators, media, and partner organizations. items.body: Metanoia, Yulianna Avdeeva’s new album for Pentatone, focuses on the transformation of Liszt’s style between his Weimar and late periods. Liszt had already shown an experimental curiosity with structure and form in the Sonata in B minor—a work presented here alongside later pieces such as the Bagatelle sans tonalité and Nuages gris. Metanoia Amazon Presto Apple Given the many versions available, Avdeeva’s B minor sonata is impressive. Some renditions are either entirely too heavy or too light, but hers strikes a sensible balance of power, speed, and musicality. There are admittedly some moments where velocity comes at the expense of clarity, but the furious and urgent spirit is aptly captured. Avdeeva shows firm command in the first section (track 1). The octave passages are bold and brash, while the runs remain light, agile, and effortless. I did find the lead-up to the second theme somewhat rushed: the Grandioso (track 2) is rousing but needs more breadth for us to fully appreciate the arrival of the D major section—something Argerich’s 1971 recording does so well. The more tender moments of the section, however, are exquisitely rendered with translucent passagework. Fortunately, Avdeeva does not rush the Andante (track 3). Its blend of nostalgia, reverie, and introspection offers a much-needed respite from the frenetic parts of the sonata and leaves enough space for the return of drama in the finale. The fugue (track 4), meticulous in its rhythm and articulation, gives a powerful drive back to the recapitulation but never leaves us with any sense of uncomfortable volatility. The late works begin with La lugubre gondola II (track 5), whose origins are as dark as the music. In 1882, Liszt is said to have had an eerie vision that his son-in-law Richard Wagner would die and that his body would be carried on a black gondola. The vision came true a few months later, in early 1883. Avdeeva reflects the grim nature of this realization as she highlights the starkness of the sparse textures and the austerity, foreboding, and finality of the monophony. The work is as much an homage to Wagner as it is a premonition, and the second half is where we hear more elements of tonality and lyricism. R.W. – Venezia (track 9), the companion work to La lugubre gondola, was written after Wagner’s death. While just as somber and still minimalistic, the piece lies largely in the lower register. Avdeeva gives the left-hand octave ostinato plenty of depth but also a necessary sense of severity. The brighter Bagatelle sans tonalité (track 6) recalls the showmanship of earlier works, though the bravado now takes the form of a more elegant virtuosity. The unmistakable element of caprice is well evoked. Yulianna Avdeeva. Photo © Kevin Kinzley. Nuages gris (track 7), like La lugubre gondola, has sinister undertones amid its minimalism. Avdeeva still finds a way to create some breathtaking tone colors; the final two mysterious chords are a good example, offering a fleeting sense of whimsy quite different from the ominous mood that pervades most of the piece. The Hungarian Rhapsody No. 17 (track 10), written just a few years before Liszt’s death, diverges considerably in character from the earlier rhapsodies, Nos. 1–15. The flamboyant, fiery, and playful profile gives way to more ominous undertones and an atonal base. Avdeeva brings out a threatening and even aggressive nature: accents and dissonances carry a stinging sharpness, and the octave passages at the end are adamant and tumultuous. Unstern! – Sinistre (track 11) is perhaps the most jarring of the late pieces, owing to its harsh atonality and even harsher textures. The accents and chords here are abrasive (as they should be), yet never become too strident on the ears. Unlike some of the other works, whose endings offer some form of catharsis, the latter sections here only prolong the doubt and disquiet, a distinction Avdeeva makes clear. The juxtaposition of works from different eras is well judged. In one sitting, the heavy mood of the late works may become a bit overbearing, but this only goes to show the effectiveness of Avdeeva’s interpretations. All in all, a series of excellent performances that should find a place on the shelf of any Liszt enthusiast. items.body: Ductape Faded Flowers Swiss Dark Nights Turkish duo Ductape have been gathering a following on the basis of a steady stream of singles and albums, in a very of the moment sound. More than anything, the duo of Çağla Güleray and Furkan Güleray have found a style that sits between the gloomy darkwave of She Past Away and the more light fast-moving quirky post-punk that we’ve come to associate with Molchat Doma and their ilk, with a touch of modern electro-darkwave for taste. And while their latest LP Faded Flowers is certainly very au courant in terms of the songwriting and performances, there’s also no denying that the band have a talent for it. Listening to cuts like “Figures” or “Gölgesiz” should give a good idea of Ductape at their most straightforward; there’s a strong propulsive bassline backed by stiff kicks and gated snares, plenty of tremelo’d guitar lines and the charismatic vocals of Güleray, who imbues her low moans and whoas with plenty of muscle. It’s a sound the band never stray too far from, but keep fairly fluid, adding in some synth leads (as on the zippy “Delilik”) or touches of other styles (the italo-infused intro of “Burn”) to taste. And while the record does have a certain sameyness to it, it’s fast-moving and has enough switch-ups to keep things moving, such as placing the occasional combo-breaker like the oompah-cabaret stylings of “Velvet Dawn” into the middle of the album. That said, the band’s bag of tricks has its limits, and multiple listens will show some of their weaker tendencies. A big one would be their general production sensibility: the bass and guitar sounds don’t vary much, their drum programming leans on eighties drum machine toms for fills to the point of distraction, and Güleray, for her confidence and power always sits in the same place in the mix, always up front, never varying in dynamics or range. To that point, these songs are often short of an actually memorable hook, usually relying on simple repeated keyboard licks or a simple refrain to fill the role. The fact is that even on multiple listens songs will tend to melt into one another, with only a few really standing out by virtue of having a vastly different tempo or arrangement. “Sad Gravity” is perhaps the most interesting song simply by virtue of using some more fully-fleshed out electronics and touches of spanish guitar. You can see why folks would enjoy a record like Faded Flowers, it’s got a sound with proven appeal, performed expertly and with enough verve to wallpaper its musical shortcomings. Having it on is never unpleasant, and it’ll no doubt have folks dancing at your local goth club, but there’s simply not enough substance here to rise above perfectly fine. Ductape are a band that probably have a really good record in them, and it’ll be interesting to see how they get there from here. Buy it. items.body: Tear a piece of this and shove it hard into your mouth A lilylicker sounds like a particularly devoted suck-up, someone whose admiration has become a full-time occupation. Put the word beside Oscar Wilde’s fascination with actresses Lillie Langtry and Sarah Bernhardt, and a whole society of worshippers comes into view: flowers, flattery, beautiful women placed upon pedestals. Wilde was a cunning linguist, of course, though Patriarchy have a few suggestions about putting that talent to more practical use. The lily remains a lovely flower, of course, though its innocence becomes somewhat harder to maintain once somebody starts licking it. The Los Angeles snuff-pop duo of Actually Huizenga and AJ English, otherwise known as The Drummer, premieres the video for Lilylicker, taken from their new EP, Appendices. Written and produced by Huizenga and English, the song takes its initial inspiration from Wilde’s devotion to those celebrated performers, then puts the woman receiving all that attention in charge of the proceedings. A menacing bass synth and a blunt kick drum set the terms, leaving Actually’s near-whispered vocal close enough to feel conspiratorial. Her poetic purr slips between the beats before the track opens into a metallic industrial-techno rhythm, bringing the hard physicality of ’90s industrial into contact with contemporary darkwave. The bass keeps its grip while crushed guitars tear through the chorus, making the move from intimate persuasion to open command feel deliciously abrupt. The words play a similar game. Wanting to be liked becomes wanting to be licked; affection, appetite, and obedience get tangled in the same exchange. Actually moves from seeking approval to prescribing exactly how it should be delivered, with an impatience that gives the song its humor. For all the literary ancestry, the central proposition is straightforward: admiration should have practical applications. Directed by Patriarchy and shot by Hazel Hill McCarthy, the video makes that business of putting people on pedestals unusually literal. Figures revolve on small platforms against an almost uninterrupted black background, their costumes and gestures exposed by direct light. Actually appears in a white gown holding lilies, in a pale pink dress draped with chains, and in a metallic corset with enormous gold wings and a guitar. English handles a skull while wearing little white wings; their young son appears in family tableaux and as a cherub perched on a classical column. The arrangements suggest devotional statues brought to life by people with their own ideas about sainthood. There is an affectionate absurdity to these living ornaments. The solemn poses give way to movement, expressions change, and the family portrait keeps interrupting the fantasy of immaculate statuary. Against all that black space, the slightest human detail becomes conspicuous. Even the insects have supporting roles. The setting came about through necessity. According to the band, the owner of their original studio location objected to the proposed content and the presence of their son, who was also appearing in the video. With the shoot abruptly displaced, the crew relocated to the Angeles woods and rethought the production outdoors. Huizenga subsequently edited the footage “happily alone and for many hours,” describing editing as “one of my secret pleasures.” “I decided not to retouch anything either. So all razor bumps, dark circles, cellulite, and sock lines are fully visible if you wish to judge me physically… I had a baby, so kill me! The boys are perfect though. A lot of the things that went ‘wrong’ ultimately added to the beauty of it, like having to shoot outside, where moths kept flying in front of our lenses, drawn in by the bright lights” For Huizenga, leaving those imperfections intact also connects to Patriarchy’s larger, apocalyptic view of power: “Patriarchy has never been about perfection, it’s about realizing we are the last remnants of human existence before AI enslaves us all; that’s why the project is called Patriarchy after all, patriarchy is the final human ruling order. Our next masters wont be women or men or human in any form, so we need to embrace our chaos and imperfections while we can.” Watch the video for Lilylicker below: Released in the wilting days of this past Summer, Appendices brings together five songs developed across different periods of the band’s life, reaching back to The Unself sessions and forward through the aftermath of 2025’s Manual For Dying. These recordings have survived abandoned versions, rewrites, and changes substantial enough to turn industrial tracks into orchestral ballads and minimal synth into metal. Alongside Lilylicker, the EP includes Bite Marks, Servile, Ode (to an Apprehensive Tyrant), and Hate Fuck, with additional production and mixing contributions across the record from Ben Chisolm and Matia Simovich. Huizenga’s reading supplies another connection between these otherwise unruly songs. Wilde, Marchesa Luisa Casati, Emperor Tiberius, and the Manson family furnish starting points for examinations of sexuality, submission, obsession, and violence. Across three full-length albums, a live record, and numerous remixes, Patriarchy have pursued those interests through industrial electronics, synth-pop, metal, and performance art. Appendices also documents Huizenga and English becoming an increasingly self-contained production team, with Lilylicker pointing toward the club without surrendering their taste for theatrical excess. That appetite for the personal and the unruly carries into Actually’s Sex and the Pity, Huizenga’s new podcast and livestream concept, whose pilot is announced for this Friday at 10 p.m. Pacific. Pitched as Elvira meeting Gore Vidal, it promises secret guests, fireside conversation, and previously untold stories from Patriarchy’s tours and beyond, forming a living journal for a future film project. “I can only really seem to recount these hilarious stories properly when I’m talking one-on-one with a cute gay at a party; so I’m gonna try to recreate that free-form energy for the podcast.” Listen to Lilylicker below and order the Appendices EP here. items.body: London duo Placebo release the single “Helen Keller” on 28 September 2026, the same day their 30th Anniversary Tour opened in Porto. The song reworks the piano melody of “H.K. Farewell,” the hidden instrumental from the band’s self-titled 1996 debut album, into a new rock track. “Helen Keller” was recorded in London and produced by Placebo together with Adam Noble, who also mixed it. Placebo ‘Helen Keller’ Brian Molko described the song as “a new rock song inspired by the piano melody from ‘H.K. Farewell'” and said it is named after one of his favourite people from history. The single is out now on streaming platforms. The 30th Anniversary Tour opened at the Super Bock Arena in Porto on 28 September and continues in Lisbon, with the setlist drawing on Placebo’s first two albums, “Placebo” (1996) and “Without You I’m Nothing” (1998), including songs the band has not performed regularly in over two decades. Placebo has confirmed that “Helen Keller” will be played live during the tour. UK and Ireland dates follow in late November and early December, including Nottingham, Glasgow and London, with a Latin American leg set for February-March 2027 covering Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Colombia and Mexico. About Placebo Placebo formed in London in 1994 after vocalist-guitarist Brian Molko and bassist-guitarist Stefan Olsdal met at South Kensington tube station. The pair first performed together as Ashtray Heart before adopting the name Placebo. The band released its self-titled debut album in 1996 through Elevator Music, followed by “Without You I’m Nothing” (1998), “Black Market Music” (2000), “Sleeping with Ghosts” (2003), “Meds” (2006), “Battle for the Sun” (2009), “Loud Like Love” (2013) and “Never Let Me Go” (2022). Matt Lunn has drummed with the band since 2015. On 11 April 2026 Placebo announced “RE:CREATED,” a reworking of the 1996 debut album produced from its original master tapes, led by the single “Nancy Boy (Re:created Version).” “Helen Keller,” released 28 September 2026 as the band’s 30th Anniversary Tour opened in Porto, extends that anniversary chronology with a new song built from a 1996-era melody.

items.body: Dark synthwave producer Das Mörtal releases the two-track single “DRAIN ME” on Lisbon Lux Records on 30 September 2026. The single pairs the original version with a remix by synthwave producer Dan Terminus, and precedes Das Mörtal’s mini-album “DECVY I,” out 29 October 2026. Das Mörtal, the project of Montreal-based producer Cristóbal Cortes, describes “DRAIN ME” as “a track about the feeling of running in circles in the health care system while being drained from the multiple tests one person might go through.” The track opens with a cinematic, sweeping tone before shifting into a fast-paced, techno-driven rhythm section with an arpeggiated synth pluck, washed-out vocals and a half-time breakdown before its final chorus. Dan Terminus, grouped alongside Perturbator, Carpenter Brut and GosT as one of what press materials call the “Four Horsemen of Synthwave,” reworks “DRAIN ME” with chopped and manipulated vocals, punchy percussion and an occasional violin line over booming basslines that combine acoustic and synthesised elements. “DRAIN ME” follows the double single “Parasite & Ghost,” which Das Mörtal released on Lisbon Lux Records on 4 June 2026, also ahead of “DECVY I.” An official teaser for “DRAIN ME” is available on YouTube, and the single is available to pre-save via ffm.to/drainmee. About Das Mörtal Das Mörtal is the project of Cristóbal Cortes, an electronic music producer and DJ based in Montreal whose work began in Berlin, drawing on artists including Steve Moore and Aphex Twin. Das Mörtal’s sound blends techno, occult electro and Italo disco into a dark, nostalgic style informed by German techno as well as horror and science-fiction soundtracks. Das Mörtal has released material including the double single “Parasite & Ghost” (2026), the “Bury the Sorrow” and “Hotline Miami II” EPs, and the “Miami Beach Witches” album, among other releases on Bandcamp. The project has performed close to 100 shows since 2015, including more than 70 dates across the United States and Europe, at festivals such as Osheaga, Transmusicales de Rennes, FME and MEG Festival, and on tour with Vitalic, Perturbator and Carpenter Brut. “DRAIN ME” is Das Mörtal’s second single of 2026 on Lisbon Lux Records, after “Parasite & Ghost” in June.

items.body: Norwegian gothic industrial metal act Gothminister release the album “We Are All Demons” on 16 October 2026 via Elevator Records, distributed through The Orchard. The 11-track record is the project’s ninth studio album. Frontman Bjørn Alexander Brem recorded, produced, mixed and mastered “We Are All Demons” entirely himself, the first time he has handled the full process alone. Musically, the album combines gothic industrial metal with EDM elements, synthesizers, industrial guitars, theatrical vocals, female duets and choral passages. Lyrically, it addresses inner darkness and the parts of the self normally kept beneath the surface. Tracklist: Darkest Side of Earth We Are All Demons Nightmare King The Dark The Spell Welcome to Hell Salsa My Revenge Darkness Is My Throne Fearless There’s a Crown for All “We Are All Demons” follows the single “My Revenge,” released from the album on 31 July 2026. The album is available for pre-order via The Orchard’s smart link. A digipak CD edition is also listed through Napalm Records’ webshop. Gothminister has confirmed the following live dates around the release: Tour dates for Gothminister’s ‘We Are All Demons’ release 16 October 2026: Fiskepiren, Stavanger, Norway 19 November 2026: Parkteatret, Oslo, Norway 20-21 November 2026: Hellsinki Industrial Festival, Helsinki, Finland More dates are expected to be announced. About Gothminister Gothminister was formed in Oslo, Norway, in 1999 by Bjørn Alexander Brem, who handles lead vocals, programming and instruments. Guitarist Glenn Nilsen is the project’s other current member. The band’s studio discography includes “Gothic Electronic Anthems” (2003), “Empire of Dark Salvation” (2005), “Happiness in Darkness” (2008), “Anima Inferna” (2011), “Utopia” (2013), “The Other Side” (2017), “Pandemonium” (2022) and “Pandemonium II: The Battle of the Underworlds” (2024). Gothminister was also a candidate in Norway’s 2024 Eurovision Song Contest selection, Melodi Grand Prix. “We Are All Demons” follows “Pandemonium II: The Battle of the Underworlds” from 2024 and arrives 16 October 2026 via Elevator Records.

items.body: New Order released their fourth studio album, “Brotherhood,” through Factory Records on 29 September 1986. The Manchester band split the record’s two sides between guitar-driven post-punk and synth-pop electronics. “Brotherhood” turns 40 this year. New Order recorded “Brotherhood” during 1986 at Jam Studios in London, Windmill Lane Studios in Dublin and Amazon Studios in Liverpool, with Michael Johnson engineering and the band credited as its own producer. The sleeve, designed by Peter Saville, photographed a sheet of titanium-zinc alloy. The album opens with a rock-facing first side – “Paradise,” “Weirdo,” “As It Is When It Was,” “Broken Promise” and “Way of Life” – before turning electronic on side two with “Bizarre Love Triangle,” “All Day Long,” “Angel Dust” and “Every Little Counts.” “Bizarre Love Triangle” became a top 20 hit in Australia and New Zealand and remains the album’s only single. “Brotherhood” streams on Spotify. About New Order New Order formed in Manchester in 1980, after singer Ian Curtis’s death ended Joy Division, when surviving members Bernard Sumner, Peter Hook and Stephen Morris continued as a trio and were joined that October by keyboardist Gillian Gilbert. The band’s debut single, “Ceremony,” a song written in Joy Division’s final weeks, appeared in January 1981, and the debut album “Movement” followed on Factory Records that November. “Power, Corruption & Lies” (1983) pushed the band further into synthesizers and sequencers, and its non-album single “Blue Monday” became the best-selling 12-inch single in UK chart history. “Low-Life” (1985) refined that mix of guitars and electronics on tracks including “The Perfect Kiss” and “Sub-culture.” “Brotherhood” arrived on 29 September 1986, dividing its rock and dance instincts across two album sides. New Order’s early singles, including those surrounding “Brotherhood,” were gathered the following year on the compilation “Substance” (1987), and the band reached UK number one with “Technique” in 1989. New Order also co-owned Manchester’s Haçienda nightclub with Factory Records, a venture whose costs contributed to the label’s 1992 collapse alongside labelmates Happy Mondays. The band moved to London Records for “Republic” (1993), split in 1993, reunited in 1998, and released “Get Ready” in 2001. Peter Hook left in 2007 following disputes with the rest of the band, and New Order continued as a quartet, releasing “Music Complete” in 2015 and the “Be a Rebel” single and remix EP in 2020 and 2021. In 2026, Joy Division and New Order were announced as joint inductees into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, with the ceremony set for November. “Brotherhood,” the record that opened New Order’s run of transatlantic hits, turns 40 this year.

items.body: Seattle darkwave project The Phantom Eyes released a video for its cover of DEVO’s “Puppet Boy,” directed by Tori Kellogg (credited as GR4VES), on 25 September 2026. DEVO’s original “Puppet Boy” appeared on the 1984 album “Shout.” The Phantom Eyes is the recording name of Bex Delgado, who released the cover in May 2026 before the video followed in September. Puppet Boy by The Phantom Eyes The Phantom Eyes’ video for ‘Puppet Boy’ Kellogg filmed the video in a single evening, building the look around red lighting, CRT distortion and VHS-style degradation. Delgado described the story behind the cover: “I was trying to embody the spirit of not exactly a dom/sub relationship, but more like a master/servant one. This story isn’t romantic in nature, but still has that sweet feeling that the characters do take care of each other.” About The Phantom Eyes The Phantom Eyes is the Seattle-based recording project of Bex Delgado, mixes darkwave and dark electronic music with post-punk elements. Delgado describes the project’s focus as horror, isolation and existential dread. The cover of DEVO’s “Puppet Boy,” released in May 2026, is one of the project’s singles; its video, filmed by Tori Kellogg and released 25 September 2026, is the most recent visual release under the project’s name.

His music centres on post-punk and dream pop, with hypnagogic pop and synthwave textures. He released his debut album, “Monochrom,” on 4 April 2025, writing, producing and handling the visual side of the record entirely on his own. The eight-track album, centred on routine, overwork and stagnation, comprises “Wszystko jest szare,” “Nawiedzony dom,” “Slasher,” “24/7,” “Za wszystko,” “Zimno,” “Sen” and “Apogeum.” Walkusz’s second album, “Fantometyka,” is due in spring 2027. “Syrena,” released 25 September 2026 and featuring Julia Frycz, is its first single.

items.body: Italian industrial darkwave act This Eternal Decay release the single and video “Violate” on 2 October 2026. Riccardo Sabetti, who handles the project’s contacts and booking, announced the release ahead of its arrival. This Eternal Decay previously released the singles “The Heart of a Lover” in 2023 and “Rise & Fall” in 2024, alongside the 2023 album “Absolution.” “Violate” is the act’s latest single since then. About This Eternal Decay This Eternal Decay is an Italian industrial darkwave project. Side-Line has covered the act since 2023, when it released the album “Absolution” and its lead single, followed by “The Heart of a Lover” the same year and “Rise & Fall” in 2024. “Violate,” out 2 October 2026, is the project’s newest single and video.

items.body: This new release from the Belgian act Hybryds is a remarkable record. The title leaves little to the imagination, focusing—as the work of many artists across various disciplines has so often done—on the seven deadly sins. What makes this release particularly intriguing, however, is that four of the tracks date back to 2002, originally appearing on the “Lust”-EP released by Spectre. After all these years, the original singer, Miss Poly-Ester, got back in touch with Sandy Nijs and asked him to complete the album. So Sandy returned to the music, and the lost tracks were finally completed with the singer’s vocals. In total, we are treated to eleven tracks. Alongside the songs addressing the seven deadly sins, there are extras such as an intro and two live tracks dating from 2003. Hybryds has continued to surprise me in recent years. The project remains true to its trademark Ritualistic style, yet everything sounds more modern. This record stands out in particular for its slow, infectious, Trip-Hop-like rhythms. At times, I get the impression of hearing an Industrial version of Tricky—and that is very much intended as a huge compliment. After all, Hybryds naturally retains that familiar industrial DNA. The atmosphere remains dark, mysterious, and unsettling, evoking the feeling of stepping into a forbidden place where a certain decadence gradually sweeps you away. This impression is further reinforced by the artistic and highly explicit booklet accompanying the album, allowing Sandy Nijs to indulge his interest in and inspiration from fetish culture through a series of photographs that remain closely connected to the central theme. It is the kind of booklet that algorithms would rapidly detect and block instantly. Fortunately, there are still artists daring enough to go there—artists for whom it isn’t simply about nudity, provocation, or shock value. The music is far too good for that. I wouldn’t claim that Hybryds have reinvented themselves, but in recent years they have clearly been riding a new wave of inspiration, and this record is a fine example of where that has taken them. The older live tracks don’t exactly add much value, but the rest of the album is simply magnificent. As far as I’m concerned, it’s one of the best albums I’ve discovered this year. It would be a true sin to let this particular gem pass you by… (Ratring:9). Listen to “Envy”: Envy by Hybryds About Hybryds Hybryds is a Belgian project centered on Sandy Nys, active since the mid-1980s and known for ritual, mythical and industrial electronic work rooted in the cassette-era Belgian underground. Nys’ career began with the 1986 cassette “Mythical Music From The 21st Century,” followed by releases including “Music For Rituals” (1992) and “The Ritual Of The Rave” (1995). In the 1990s Hybryds became a duo with Leen Smets (Yasnaïa); from 2000 Nys continued the project solo before German vocalist Madeline joined, with multi-instrumentalist Peter De Koning later expanding the lineup. On 3RioArt / Zoharum, Hybryds has released “Mythopia” (2022), “Mythopia, The Sequel” (2024), “In The Wake Of The Witch” (2025), “Fire And Ice, Flesh And Bones Part 1 & 2” (2026) and “Desert Of White Salt” (2026). “7even Deadly Sins” follows on the same labels, reworking four tracks that originally appeared on the 2002 “Lust” EP on Spectre with new vocals by Madeline and Katherina.

items.body: Cork, Ireland duo Crá Croí release the single “Just Another Day” on 2 October 2026, on Bandcamp and streaming platforms. It is the third and last single from the duo’s debut album, “Tá Brón Orm,” due 30 October 2026. “Just Another Day” addresses what the duo describe as a cynical view of modern life, where emotions feel performative and authenticity is replaced by “superficial substitutes.” Crá Croí is entirely self-produced by the duo, credited as RG and CD, who also direct their own videos and artwork. Side-Line previously covered the duo’s single “Lord Of The Wild” in July 2026. About Crá Croí Crá Croí is a Cork, Ireland duo whose name translates from Irish as “torment of the heart.” The project is self-produced from music to visuals by its two members, credited as RG and CD. Side-Line covered the duo’s single “Lord Of The Wild” in July 2026. “Just Another Day,” released 2 October 2026, is the third and final single from the duo’s debut album, “Tá Brón Orm,” due 30 October 2026.
